record.label: Full support by contact and local curvature
record.statement: For an admissible pure zero-field SK minimizer, its Stieltjes support is [0,1). A finite-chord comparison using q(0)=0, q<=1 and strict zero-interval convexity excludes empty support; contact and positive-plateau curvature exclude bounded gaps; zero-plateau curvature excludes an initial gap. At a last support point r, the terminal chord obstruction gives q(t)<t and G(r)<0, contradicting atom addition. Consequently q(t)=t and E[Phi_xx(t,X_t)^2]=1 for 0<=t<1. This alternate proof does not use the quantitative terminal defect estimate.
record.boundary: Ordinary authored deduction checked against retained mathematical inputs; no new Lean declaration, elaborated dependency, cross-model transport, Comparator acceptance or independent proof certification is asserted.

aligned_passages.text: **Theorem 5.1 (full support).** In the pure zero-field SK model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimize $\mathcal P$. Then $\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1)$ and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing. For every associated diffusion started at zero, $\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2=t$ and $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ for $0\le t<1$. Keep the same minimiser, diffusion and moment function $q$ throughout. Section 3 has established $G\ge0$, $G=0$ on the support $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$, and the contact conditions $q(s)=s$, $q'(s)\le1$ at support points. At zero, the value identity comes from symmetry, and the slope bound requires $0\in S$. Section 4 supplies curvature on constant intervals for every admissible coefficient. These premises are available before any support gap is excluded. We first deal with the endpoint at one, then use the curvature estimate on the remaining intervals. For a terminal interval $(a,1)$, including empty support $[0,1)$, the cusp estimate gives $1-q(t)\gtrsim\sqrt{1-t}$ and hence $G<0$ near one. On a positive plateau with two contact endpoints, strict convexity puts $q'$ below its endpoint chord, although its integral must equal the interval length. On a zero plateau the heat argument makes $q'$ strictly increasing, below the right contact slope. At an initial gap, use the one-sided contact slope if $0\in S$; otherwise the coefficient is zero and symmetry supplies $q(0)=0$. **Why a terminal plateau violates the variational inequality.** Suppose that $\gamma=c$ on $(a,1)$, where $0\le a<1$ and $c\ge0$ is finite. The endpoint $1$ is outside the support domain, so there is no contact condition there to complete an endpoint-chord argument. Instead we will prove $$ 1-q(t)\ge C\sqrt{1-t} \tag{5.1} $$ for some $C>0$ and every $t$ sufficiently close to one. The proof separates two facts: the diffusion puts positive probability density near zero, and the smoothed terminal slope has a definite deficit from $\pm1$ in a shrinking window around zero. Fix $s\in(a,1)$ and let $\rho_s$ be the law of $X_s$. Choose $R<\infty$ such that $p_0=\rho_s([-R,R])>0$. For $c>0$, set $$ h(t,y)=\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt{1-t}Z|},\qquad \Phi(t,y)=c^{-1}\log h(t,y), $$ where $Z$ is standard normal. The drift on this interval is $c\Phi_x=h_x/h$, and the transition density is $$ k_{s,t}(x,y)=p_{t-s}(y-x)\frac{h(t,y)}{h(s,x)},\qquad p_v(z)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/(2v)}. \tag{5.2} $$ The heat-semigroup identity normalises this kernel; equivalently, for Brownian motion started at $(s,x)$, $h(t,B_t)/h(s,x)$ is the positive mean-one change of measure which adds the drift $h_x/h$. For $c=0$, the same kernel formula applies with $h=1$, and the value function is the ordinary heat evolution of $|x|$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, proof of (6.6)][fs-var]. Put $L=1-s$ and $\delta=L/2$. For $s+\delta\le t<1$, $|x|\le R$ and $|y|\le1$, $$ p_{t-s}(y-x)\ge (2\pi L)^{-1/2}e^{-(R+1)^2/(2\delta)}=:k_*>0, $$ while $h(t,y)\ge1$ and $h(s,x)\le e^{cR}\mathbb E e^{c\sqrt L|Z|}=:M<\infty$. Integrating (5.2) over the part of $\rho_s$ in $[-R,R]$ therefore gives a density $f_t$ of $X_t$ with $$ f_t(y)\ge p_0k_*/M=:m>0 \quad(s+\delta\le t<1,\ |y|\le1). \tag{5.3} $$ Only positive mass of a compact set was needed at time $s$; no density assumption on $\rho_s$ has entered. Now write $\varepsilon=1-t$ and restrict to $|y|\le\sqrt\varepsilon$. Differentiating the terminal heat formula gives, with the unweighted interpretation for $c=0$, $$ u(t,y)= \frac{\mathbb E[\operatorname{sgn}(y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z) e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}]} {\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}}. $$ The denominator is at most $D=e^c\mathbb E e^{c|Z|}<\infty$. Each sign has unnormalised mass at least $p_*:=\mathbb P(Z\ge1)>0$: the threshold $|y/\sqrt\varepsilon|$ is at most one, and the exponential weight is at least one. Hence each sign has tilted probability at least $\theta=p_*/D\in(0,1/2)$. It follows that $$ |u(t,y)|\le1-2\theta,\qquad 1-u(t,y)^2\ge4\theta(1-\theta)=:\kappa>0. $$ Multiplying this uniform deficit by the density lower bound (5.3) and the window width $2\sqrt\varepsilon$ yields $$ 1-q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}(1-u(t,y)^2)f_t(y)\,dy \ge 2m\kappa\sqrt{1-t}. $$ This proves (5.1) with $C=2m\kappa$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, density and terminal-window estimates][fs-var]. The sign of the contradiction is now explicit. For $s'$ sufficiently close to one, the estimate holds at every $t\in[s',1)$, so $$ \begin{aligned} G(s')&=\int_{s'}^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\\ &\le\frac{(1-s')^2}{2} -\frac{2C}{3}(1-s')^{3/2}<0. \end{aligned} $$ The final inequality holds once $\sqrt{1-s'}<4C/3$. It contradicts the nonnegative cost of adding an atom at $s'$. This proof covers $c=0$ as well as $c>0$. In particular, empty support is impossible: then $\mu_\gamma=0$ and $\gamma=0$ on all of $[0,1)$. The terminal-plateau conclusion was already recorded in [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Remark 7][acz]; the estimates above supply the quantitative argument needed here. The terminal gap is now excluded. The [zero-interval argument](#zero-plateau) makes $q$ strictly convex on $[0,1)$, whereas the positive-plateau argument above makes $q'$ strictly convex. Here $q(0)=0$ and $0\le q\le1$. Its complement is a union of relative open intervals, and the Stieltjes measure vanishes on each such interval. For $x First consider a gap $(a,b)$ with both endpoints in $S$, allowing $a=0$. Compact-strip regularity gives continuity of $q'$ on $[a,b]$, even if $\gamma$ jumps at an endpoint. Contact gives $$ q(a)=a,\qquad q(b)=b,\qquad q'(a),q'(b)\le1. \tag{5.4} $$ If the constant coefficient is $c>0$, Section 4 makes $q'$ strictly convex in the gap. Continuity extends the chord comparison to its endpoints, giving $$ q'(t)<\frac{b-t}{b-a}q'(a)+\frac{t-a}{b-a}q'(b)\le1, \qquad a With $h=q'$ and $C_{a,b}$ its endpoint chord, the contradiction is the exact area identity $$ (b-a)-\int_a^b h =(b-a)\left(1-\frac{h(a)+h(b)}2\right) +\int_a^b(C_{a,b}-h)>0. $$ The first term is nonnegative; strict convexity makes the second positive. Only continuity of $q'$ is needed at the ends. For example, a jump $\Delta\gamma$ at $s$ gives the one-sided identity $$ q''(s+)-q''(s-)=-2\Delta\gamma\,\mathbb E a(s,X_s)^3. $$ It follows by applying Itô's formula to $a^2$ and using continuity of its derivative moments on a compact strip. Taking $\gamma=0$ before $s=1/2$ and $\gamma=1/2$ afterward makes this jump strictly negative; the terminal Cole–Hopf solution has positive Hessian. Thus continuity of $q'$ does not license classical higher time derivatives across coefficient jumps. [OpenAI (2026a), proof of Corollary 6.4][fs-density]. If $(0,b)$ is a gap and $0\in S$, the preceding proof applies using the one-sided contact slope bound at zero. Because $(0,b)$ contains no mass, the support condition at zero forces an atom there and hence $c=\gamma(0)>0$. Its absence has not been proved at this stage. If instead the complementary component is $[0,b)$ with $0\notin S$, there is no mass anywhere in $[0,b)$. Thus $\gamma=0$ there. The identity $q(0)=0$ comes from zero-field symmetry, and the right endpoint gives $q(b)=b$, $q'(b)\le1$. Therefore $$ \gamma(b)-\gamma(a)=\mu_\gamma((a,b])>0 \qquad(0\le a0$ is already impossible: either $h\le1$ everywhere, forcing $h\equiv1$ by its integral, or it attains an interior maximum above one, where $h'=0$ and $h''\le0$. This is an elementary deduction from these premises. Chen's conditional crossing theorem, with its own hypotheses, is of this form; §4 proves the stronger $q'''>0$ throughout a positive plateau, without a minimizer premise. See [Chen, arXiv:2607.18032v1, Proposition 4.2 and the proof of Proposition 4.3][chen26]. Neither statement supplies terminal contact at the excluded endpoint one.

**Abstract.** The Stieltjes measure of every integrable minimiser of the
zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure, zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has full support on $[0,1)$ and a smooth
density that is strictly positive on $(0,1)$. We reconstruct OpenAI's quantitative
argument, organised around two uses of one spatial-moment inequality.
On a positive constant interval, it makes the derivative of the gradient
second moment strictly convex, contradicting the endpoint conditions
imposed by minimality. The same curvature and the bounded gradient
also exclude terminal gaps. Full support then gives moment identities and
smoothness; a local constant replacement transfers the inequality to the minimiser and
forces its density to be positive. H.-B. Chen previously proved full support
and smooth nonnegative density. We isolate the fixed-time spatial moment
and the positive margin that survives local replacement, while importing its
shape comparisons and full polynomial identity. We also derive the scalar value
identity and explain its classical optimisation consequence. For the quantum approximate
optimization algorithm (QAOA), we identify the rooted energy of a finite Gaussian
observable and the separate circuit theorem that approximates it. A further
second-moment theorem gives a measured near-optimal configuration on the same
random instance, with the circuit word fixed before the number of spins grows.

[Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1][ACZ] proved infinite support. This need not be full support: the measure $\sum_{k\geq1}2^{-k}\delta_{1-2^{-k}}$ has infinitely many atoms and many gaps. [H.-B. Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][Chen] subsequently proved full support and smooth nonnegative density. We follow OpenAI's quantitative proof of the support conclusion and its further strict-positivity result. The feature used twice is a lower bound valid throughout every positive constant interval of an admissible coefficient, without a minimising assumption. **Theorem 1 (full support; quantitative proof following [OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][FS]).** If $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimises $\mathcal P$, then $$ \operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1),\qquad \gamma(t_2)>\gamma(t_1)\quad(0\leq t_10$, with probability tending to one there are configurations $\sigma,\tau$ with $|R(\sigma,\tau)-\rho|<\delta$ and both energies at least $n(P_*-\eta)$. This follows from [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Proposition 1, equation (5)][ACZ], using the Gaussian normalisation above. Our purpose is to isolate the spatial moment common to the support and density arguments, explain why it needs an integrated estimate, and identify what survives the local-replacement limit. The conclusions and the quantitative method are those of the cited sources. The proof compares two demands on a gap with two support endpoints. Minimality forces $q$ to agree with time there, with endpoint slopes at most one. On a positive constant interval a quantitative estimate makes $q'$ strictly convex, so its integral is smaller than the interval's length. This contradicts the required change in $q$. After excluding all gaps, the identity $q'=1$ supplies the equation from which the same estimate will force $\gamma'>0$. A qualitative crossing criterion already suffices for a bounded gap. The density argument needs more: an estimate for a local constant replacement that need not minimise, at a time where $q''$ need not vanish, and a positive lower bound that survives the limit. The second aim, in §5, is to follow the support identities to a finite Gaussian observable whose rooted energy a QAOA circuit approximates, then identify the additional concentration input for a measured configuration. These optimisation consequences use full support; strict density positivity is a further analytic conclusion. Readers interested in optimisation may accept Theorem 1 and continue to §5. Sections 2–4 assume Itô calculus and martingale convergence; the circuit construction is a separate imported theorem. Omitted proofs are linked to *From Parisi full support to deterministic QAOA circuits: A long reasoning record*, the [companion edition of 26 October 2026](../long/reasoning-record.md); original-source citations remain beside the imported inputs.

The Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) model asks us to choose signs that
maximise a random sum of pair interactions. The Parisi formula expresses
the limiting maximum through a nondecreasing function, the **order
parameter**. We explain why a minimising order parameter cannot be
constant on any interval below one.

The proof compares two consequences of a hypothetical gap. Minimality
fixes the values and bounds the slopes of an auxiliary curve at its
endpoints. An analytic estimate makes the derivative strictly convex
between them, leaving too little area to connect the required values.
Initial and terminal gaps need separate arguments. We then return to
the spins: a theorem about their energies gives nearly optimal sign
choices differing on any prescribed positive fraction of positions up to one half,
with arbitrarily small error in that fraction.

We follow the quantitative proof in [OpenAI (2026a)][support-manuscript];
[Hong-Bin Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][chen-support] had already proved
full support by a different method. The estimate used here makes the
final contradiction a direct comparison of areas. We assume algebra
and elementary calculus, and introduce probability and cumulative mass
through calculations. The deeper analytic facts are stated where the
proof needs them. By the end of Sections 1–6, the reader should be able
to reconstruct how minimality and those inputs exclude each kind of gap,
then translate the result into a statement about spin configurations.
Section 7 gives optional calculations and answers to the short questions
in the text; the full analytic proofs remain in the cited sources.

## 4. The full-support theorem

**Source theorem ([OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][support-manuscript]).**
In the pure, zero-field model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma$ be an
admissible integrable minimiser of $\mathcal P$. Its Stieltjes measure
has full relative support on $[0,1)$, and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing.
For every associated diffusion and every $0\le t<1$,

$$
\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2]=t,\qquad
\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]=1.
$$

The theorem requires a minimiser,
not merely an admissible candidate. Zero field supplies $q(0)=0$;
$\xi''=1$ enters the curvature estimate. The statement does not cover
nonzero field or general mixed-spin covariance functions.

### 5.4 The remaining initial and terminal gaps **Initial gap with zero outside the support.** Suppose $[0,s)$ is missing and $s<1$ is the first support point. Then $\gamma=0$ there, so the positive-coefficient bound supplies no strictness. Instead the zero-coefficient heat identity gives $$ q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0\qquad(00$ throughout $(0,1)$: it is $q$ itself that is strictly convex. Recall that $q(0)=0$ and $q\le1$. For $00$. **The excess slope persists and violates the bound.** To control a later slope, use the same chord rule on the larger interval $[r,s]$, where $t0. $$ The bound holds at every time after $t$, so integration gives $q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))$. Choose any time $$ t+\frac{1-t}{1+h(t)}0$, and the lower bound now gives $q(s)>1$, contradicting $q(s)\le1$ strictly before time one. Thus $q(t)[§5, terminal estimate](../long/reasoning-record.md#terminal-gap). [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Remark 7][acz] had already recorded the absence of terminal plateaus. These cases exhaust the complement of the support. Contact now gives $q(t)=t$ for every interior time, and symmetry includes zero. Differentiating gives $\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]=1$, completing the theorem.
